forms.en: I have made, I have done

at lave.explanation: "At lave" is one of the most useful Danish verbs, because it covers both "make" and "do" for activities. "Hvad laver du?" means "What are you doing?", and "at lave mad" means to cook. It is different from "at gøre", which is used for "do" with a specific thing, as in "gøre noget ved det" (do something about it).

sentence.en: What are we going to do tonight?

at lave lektier.explanation: "At lave lektier" means to do homework. Danish says "make" (lave) where English says 'do'. "Lektier" only exists as a plural, so you never say 'a lektie' for homework. Many people just say "jeg laver lektier" to mean they are studying after school.

sentence.en: The children do homework after school.

at lave mad.explanation: "At lave mad" means to cook, and it is made of "lave" (to make) and "mad" (food). So it literally means "to make food". The verb "at koge" is more specific, meaning to boil. Use "lave mad" for any cooking, and add a dish if you want: "jeg laver pasta".

sentence.en: My father cooks every day.

at le.explanation: "At le" means to laugh, and it is a short, slightly more formal word than "at grine". "Vi lo meget" means "We laughed a lot". "Latter" is the word for laughter.

sentence.en: We laughed all evening.

at lede efter.explanation: "At lede efter" means to look for something that you cannot find yet. "Jeg leder efter mine nøgler" means "I am looking for my keys". Do not mix it up with "at se på" (to look at). The small word "efter" stays with it. The past form is "ledte efter" and the "have" form is "ledt efter".

sentence.en: I am looking for my keys.

at lege.explanation: "At lege" means to play in the way children do, just for fun: "Børnene leger i haven" (The children are playing in the garden). It is not used for sports or instruments, where Danish uses "at spille". Adults say "at lege" too when they are being playful. A toy is "et legetøj" and a playground is "en legeplads".

sentence.en: The children are playing in the garden.

at leve.explanation: "At leve" means to live in the sense of being alive. "Hun lever stadig" means "She is still alive". It is also used for how you live your life: "leve et godt liv". Do not use it for where your home is; for that Danes say "at bo". "Længe leve!" is a cheer meaning "Long live!".

sentence.en: My grandfather is still alive.

at ligge.explanation: "At ligge" means to lie, to be lying down or to be placed flat: "Bogen ligger på bordet" (The book is lying on the table). It also tells where places are, as in "Byen ligger ved havet". Do not mix it up with "at lægge", which is to put something down.

sentence.en: The book is lying on the table.

at like.explanation: "At like" is borrowed straight from English and only means pressing "like" on something online. Do not mix it up with "at kunne lide", which is the normal way to say you like a person, food or activity in real life.

sentence.en: She usually likes my pictures.

at lukke.explanation: "At lukke" means to close, for a door, a window, a shop or a bag. "Kan du lukke døren?" means "Can you close the door?". It is the opposite of "at åbne" (to open). In shops you may hear "Vi lukker om ti minutter" (We close in ten minutes).

sentence.en: Can you close the window, please?

at lytte.explanation: "At lytte" means to listen on purpose: "Jeg lytter til musik" (I am listening to music). It is normally used with "til" (to). It is different from "at høre", which is simply to hear something, whether you want to or not. Compare "Jeg hørte en lyd" (I heard a sound) with "Jeg lyttede til musikken".

sentence.en: I listen to the radio in the morning.

at låne.explanation: "At låne" means both to borrow and to lend, so the context tells you which. "Kan jeg låne din pen?" means you want to borrow it. "Jeg låner dig min cykel" means you lend it to someone. To make the meaning clear, Danes sometimes say "låne af" (borrow from) and "låne ud" (lend out).

sentence.en: Can I borrow your pen?

at lægge.explanation: "At lægge" means to lay or to put something down flat, like a book on a table or a baby in bed. "Jeg lægger bogen på bordet" means "I put the book on the table". Compare it with "at sætte" (put something so it sits up) and "at ligge" (to be lying somewhere). "Læg dig ned" means "Lie down".

sentence.en: She puts the book on the table.

at lære.explanation: "At lære" means both to learn and to teach, and the context tells you which: "Jeg lærer dansk" (I learn Danish) and "Hun lærer mig dansk" (She teaches me Danish). For the second use, you can add "at lære fra sig". A teacher is "en lærer", which looks just like "lærer" in "jeg lærer". Do not mix it up with "at læse".

sentence.en: I am learning Danish every day.

at læse.explanation: "At læse" means to read: "Jeg læser en bog" (I am reading a book). It is also the Danish word for studying a field at university, as in "Hun læser medicin" (She studies medicine). The word "læser" without "at" is a reader. Do not mix it up with "at lære" (to learn).

sentence.en: I am reading a book in bed.

at løbe.explanation: "At løbe" means to run, for sport or in a hurry: "Jeg løber hver morgen" (I run every morning). It also describes a nose or a river that flows. A fun phrase is "at løbe tør for", which means to run out of something.

sentence.en: I run in the park every morning.

en lampe.explanation: "En lampe" is a lamp. It is used for a table lamp or a floor lamp, and a ceiling light is "en loftlampe". To switch it on you say "tænd lampen", and "sluk lampen" turns it off. Lamps are everywhere in Danish homes, where soft lighting is part of the cosy feeling called "hygge".

sentence.en: Can you switch on the lamp?

en landmand.explanation: "En landmand" is a farmer. It is built from "land" (country) and "mand" (man). The word for more than one changes its vowel: "landmænd". A farm is "en gård", and farming as a trade is "landbrug". Danish farms are often family-run.

sentence.en: The farmer works in the field.

en lejlighed.explanation: "En lejlighed" is an apartment or flat. You can rent one ("at leje en lejlighed") or buy one, while a whole house is "et hus". The word is long, so say it in parts: lej-lig-hed. People often describe size by rooms, for example "en lejlighed med tre værelser".

sentence.en: We live in a small apartment.

en lillebror.explanation: "En lillebror" is a younger brother, literally "little brother". It is used for any brother who is younger than you. The older one is "en storebror". Notice the plural "lillebrødre", where the vowel changes.

sentence.en: My little brother goes to nursery school.

en lillesøster.explanation: "En lillesøster" is a younger sister, literally "little sister". It is used for any sister who is younger than you. The older one is "en storesøster". The plural is "lillesøstre".

sentence.en: My little sister loves to draw.

en liste.explanation: "Liste" is a list, just like in English. Danes make "en indkøbsliste" (a shopping list) and "en huskeliste" (a reminder list) all the time. The plural is "lister". To put something on a list you say "at skrive noget på listen".

sentence.en: I am writing a list.

en liter.explanation: "En liter" is a liter, used for milk, water and fuel. In the plural it stays "liter": "to liter mælk" (two liters of milk). Danish shops use the metric system, so you will see "liter" and "deciliter" in recipes. Half a liter is "en halv liter".

sentence.en: I am buying two liters of milk.

en lomme.explanation: "En lomme" means a pocket on clothes. You can say "Det er i min lomme" (It is in my pocket). Pocket money for children is called "lommepenge", and a flashlight is "en lommelygte". You will find it in many compound words.

sentence.en: My keys are in my pocket.

en lufthavn.explanation: En lufthavn is an airport. It is made of "luft" (air) and "havn" (harbour), so it is a harbour for the air. And "the airport" is "lufthavnen". You say "i lufthavnen" for "at the airport". The big Danish one near Copenhagen is called Kastrup.

sentence.en: We are going to the airport at six o'clock.

en læbe.explanation: "En læbe" is a lip. You will mostly use it in the form for more than one, "læber", for example "røde læber" (red lips) or "tørre læber" (dry lips). It is often a part of beauty words like "læbestift" (lipstick).

sentence.en: My lips are dry.

en læge.explanation: "En læge" is a doctor, the person you see when you are ill. In Danish you often just say "lægen" (the doctor) for your own family doctor. Remember the phrase "at gå til lægen" for going to see the doctor, and note that "en læge" can be a man or a woman.

sentence.en: I am going to the doctor tomorrow.

en lærer.explanation: "En lærer" is a teacher, someone who works at a school. The word is the same for men and women. Notice that the "the" form doubles the ending: "læreren". A tip: "at lære" means both to learn and to teach, and "en lærer" is the person who teaches.

sentence.en: Our teacher is very kind.

en løve.explanation: "En løve" is a lion. Note the letter "ø", which is said like the vowel in "bird" in English. "Løven" is "the lion". The lion is often called the king of animals, "dyrenes konge".

sentence.en: The lion roared loudly.

et land.explanation: "Et land" means a country, but it can also mean countryside or land. "På landet" means 'in the countryside', and "i udlandet" means 'abroad'. In Danish, 'the country' is "landet" and the plural is "lande". Careful with "landet": it can also mean 'the countryside'.

sentence.en: Denmark is a small country.

et liv.explanation: "Et liv" means life, both a person's life and life in general. The word does not change in the plural: "to liv" is two lives. Common phrases are "livet er godt" (life is good) and "at have et godt liv". It also appears in "i live" (alive), but that is a different thing to learn later.

sentence.da: Jeg har et godt **liv** i Danmark.
sentence.en: I have a good life in Denmark.

et lår.explanation: "Et lår" is the thigh, the top part of your leg between the hip and the knee. And the word for more than one looks the same: "to lår". Cooks use it too, for example "kyllingelår" is a chicken thigh.

sentence.en: I have pain in my thigh.

et løg.explanation: "Et løg" is an onion. The plural is the same as the singular, so "to løg" means two onions. Danes use "løg" in cooking a lot and also as a topping, for example "ristede løg" (fried onions) on a hot dog. The letter ø sounds a bit like the u in "fur".

sentence.en: I am cutting an onion.

forms.da: Lad os se, hvad klokken er.
forms.en: Let's see what time it is.

forms.da: Lad os se, om han kommer.

lad os se.explanation: "Lad os se" means "let's see" and is what you say while you think, check something or wait for a result. It is also useful as a mild "we'll find out". The word "lad" works like "let", so "lad os gå" means "let's go".

sentence.da: **Lad os se**, hvad der er i køleskabet.
sentence.en: Let's see what is in the fridge.

laks.explanation: "Laks" means salmon, the fish. It is an en-word, so "the salmon" is "laksen". It is eaten smoked ("røget laks") on bread or baked with potatoes. Notice that it needs no "a": "Jeg spiser laks".

sentence.en: I eat salmon with potatoes.

lang.explanation: "Lang" means long, in distance or in time. With an et-word it takes a "-t" (langt), and with many things it takes "-e" (lange). "Langt" on its own also means far: "Det er langt væk" is "It is far away". The opposite is "kort" (short), and "længere" means longer.

sentence.en: It is a long day.

langsom.explanation: "Langsom" means slow. Add "t" for et-words ("et langsomt tog") and "-me" for more than one: "langsomme" with a double "m". To say that something happens slowly, use "langsomt": "Tal langsomt, tak" (Speak slowly, please). A good phrase for learners to know. The opposite is "hurtig" (fast).

sentence.en: Can you speak a little more slowly?

forms.en: The hotel is far from the town.

langt fra.explanation: "Langt fra" means far from something, and the place or thing you mean comes after it. It is the opposite of "tæt på" (close to). Note that on its own "langt fra" can also be used to mean "far from it", as a way to say "not at all".

sentence.en: Our house is far from the town.

langt væk.explanation: "Langt væk" means far away. "Langt" means long or far, and "væk" means away. It is used when something is a great distance from you, whether on foot or by car. The opposite idea is "tæt på" or "i nærheden".

sentence.en: My family lives far away.

lav.explanation: "Lav" means low, and it is also used for a person who is short. With an et-word it takes "-t" (lavt), and with many things "-e" (lave). It can also describe prices: "lave priser" means low prices. The opposite is "høj", and "lavere" means lower.

sentence.en: The price is very low.

legetøj.explanation: "Legetøj" means toys as a group. In Danish it is an et-word that does not have a normal plural, so you say "mit legetøj" for "my toys". For one toy you can say "et stykke legetøj" or use a specific word like "en bamse" or "en bil".

sentence.en: The children have a lot of toys.

lektier.explanation: "Lektier" means homework. It is always used in this form, which looks like more than one, so you say "mange lektier" (a lot of homework) and "lektierne" (the homework). The usual verb is "at lave": "Jeg laver lektier". "En lektie" is one piece of homework, but it is rarely used.

sentence.en: I have a lot of homework today.

let.explanation: "Let" has two meanings: easy ("en let opgave") and light in weight ("en let taske"). Context makes it clear which one you mean. It does not change for en-words and et-words, but you add "-e" for more than one ("lette opgaver"). The opposite is "svær" (difficult) or "tung" (heavy). Also note that the other word for easy in daily talk is "nem".

sentence.en: Danish is not that easy.

lidt.explanation: "Lidt" means "a little" or "a bit" and works for both amounts and degrees, as in "lidt mælk" (a little milk) and "lidt træt" (a bit tired). It is very handy for being polite, like "Jeg taler lidt dansk". Don't mix it up with "lille" (small), which describes how big something is. "Lidt" is the opposite of "meget" (a lot).

sentence.en: I speak a little Danish.

forms.en: Can you speak a bit slower?

lidt langsommere, tak.explanation: "Lidt langsommere, tak" means "a bit slower, please" and is what a learner says when Danish is spoken too fast. "Langsom" means slow, and "langsommere" is "slower". Add "kan du sige det igen?" if you also want it repeated.

sentence.da: Jeg er ny i Danmark. **Lidt langsommere, tak.**
sentence.en: I am new in Denmark. A bit slower, please.

lige.explanation: "Lige" as a describing word means straight or equal, and it never changes its ending. It is also a very common little word meaning "just" or "right": "lige nu" is right now and "lige ved siden af" is right next to. The opposite of straight is "skæv" (crooked).

sentence.en: The street is straight.

forms.en: What are you doing right now?

lige nu.explanation: "Lige nu" means right now, at this very moment. "Nu" means now, and "lige" makes it more exact. It is very common in everyday talk. For something later, use "om lidt" (in a little while), and for a longer stretch, "for tiden" (at the moment).

sentence.en: I do not have time right now.

forms.en: He is just like his father.

ligesom.explanation: "Ligesom" means "just like" or "the same as" and is used when you compare two things that are alike. "Du er ligesom din mor" means "You are just like your mother". It can also mean "as if" in casual talk. It is stronger than "som" (like, as), because "lige" means "exactly".

sentence.en: You are just like your father.

lilla.explanation: "Lilla" means purple. It never changes its ending, so you say "en lilla bluse", "et lilla tørklæde" and "lilla blomster". It is also what you call lilac or violet shades in everyday speech.

sentence.en: I have a purple bag.

lille.explanation: "Lille" means small or little. It is a bit special: it stays "lille" with both en-words and et-words, but with many things it becomes "små" (små biler). "Mindre" means smaller. The opposite is "stor" (big). Use it with children too: "en lille dreng" is a little boy.

sentence.en: We have a small apartment.

luft.explanation: Luft is air. It is an en-word, so "the air" is "luften", and you say "i luften" for "in the air". A common phrase is "frisk luft" (fresh air), as in going outside for some. It is also the first part of "en lufthavn" (an airport), a harbour for planes.

sentence.en: I need some fresh air.

lukket.explanation: "Lukket" means closed, for doors, shops, windows and roads. It is the opposite of "åben" (open). It already ends in "t", so it stays the same for en-words and et-words, and you add "-de" for more than one: "lukkede". You will see "Lukket" on shop doors outside opening hours. The verb is "at lukke" (to close).

sentence.en: The bank is closed today.

lys.explanation: "Lys" means light or bright, and it works for colours (light colours) and for rooms or days full of daylight. Note that an et-word needs a "t": "et lyst rum". The opposite is "mørk" (dark). It also works for a thing: "et lys" is a candle or a light.

sentence.en: The kitchen is very bright in the morning.

lyseblå.explanation: "Lyseblå" means light blue. It is made from "lys" (light) and "blå" (blue) joined into one word. With et-words it gets a "t" ("et lyseblåt hus"), and with more than one it stays "lyseblå". The darker one is "mørkeblå".

sentence.en: She has a light blue shirt.

lysegrøn.explanation: "Lysegrøn" means light green. It is made of "lys" (light) and "grøn" (green) joined into one word. With et-words it gets a "t" ("et lysegrønt hus") and with more than one "ne" ("lysegrønne biler"). The darker one is "mørkegrøn".

sentence.en: She has a light green dress.

lyserød.explanation: "Lyserød" means pink. It is built from "lys" (light) and "rød" (red), so it is literally "light red". With et-words it gets a "t" ("et lyserødt hus") and with more than one an "e" ("lyserøde kjoler").

sentence.en: The child has a pink sweater.

lækker.explanation: "Lækker" means delicious or tasty, and it is the word Danes use most when they praise food. It can also mean attractive, as in "en lækker bil" (a nice car), so it is used for more than food. Look at the forms: an et-word adds "t" ("lækkert") and the plural drops the second "k" ("lækre").

sentence.en: The soup is really delicious.

længe.explanation: "Længe" means for a long time: "Jeg har ventet længe" (I have waited a long time). You often see it in questions: "Hvor længe?" is How long? It is also used in the phrase "for længe siden" (a long time ago). Do not mix it up with "lang", which describes length of things.

sentence.en: I have lived here for a long time.

lørdag.explanation: "Lørdag" is Saturday. The word "lørdag" is also used in "lørdagsgodt", the sweets that Danish children traditionally get on Saturday. Say "på lørdag" for the coming Saturday and "om lørdagen" for every Saturday. Remember the letter ø, and write day names with a small letter.

sentence.en: We do the shopping on Saturdays.
